children.text: A portfolio that has not been defined cannot be managed. PMI's portfolio standard requires every component to be identified, classified and assigned governance before anything else is done with it. That sounds obvious, yet most organizations running a transformation have never written down the complete list of what they are running.

Chapter 15 does that work for Vermont, producing a 19-component inventory. This lesson shows how the inventory was built, how each component is classified, what the exercise typically reveals, and how to build the same inventory for your own organization or state.

The book calls this exercise often the single highest-value first step toward portfolio governance. It costs little, needs no new authority, and almost always changes how leaders understand the scale of what they are doing.
Why Definition Comes First

Every later portfolio decision depends on the inventory. You cannot schedule components by dependency if you have not listed them. You cannot resolve resource conflicts between components you do not know exist. You cannot trace benefits to goals, or score risks against components, without a complete list to work from.

Vermont, the book notes, has never published such a definition. Its transformation arrives through several channels at once: statutes, a federal model agreement and its closeout, a federal grant program, and a series of agency reports. Each channel carries its own obligations and deadlines, and each tends to be owned by a different unit. Without an inventory, nobody sees them as one body of work.

That is not unique to Vermont. Initiatives in large organizations are usually owned by different departments that do not otherwise compare notes, so the total is invisible from any single seat. Defining the portfolio is the act of making it visible from one seat.

Definition also protects against double counting and silent gaps. Two units can each believe the other owns a piece of work, or both can be doing it. Writing every component down, once, with one owner, is the simplest way to find both problems before they cost a deadline.
The portfolio inventory is the foundation document of portfolio management: every component, its pillar, its owner, its type, its priority and its next stage gate, in one place.
How Vermont's 19 Components Were Found

The inventory in Figure 15.3 is HTR's own, not an official state document. It was assembled by reading Act 68, the AHEAD State Agreement, Vermont's Rural Health Transformation Program application and the AHS transformation reports, and listing every initiative that carries a named owner and a dated obligation. Each was then assigned to the pillar whose function it serves.

Two rules made the exercise work. First, an initiative only counts if it has an owner and a date; aspirations without either are not components yet. Second, each component goes to exactly one pillar, chosen by function: a data platform is Technology even if it is funded through a payment program. Applied in early 2026, the exercise produced nineteen components.

The book is careful about what the number means. Nineteen is what the exercise produced at that date. It is not a number Vermont has adopted, and anyone repeating the exercise against later reports should expect it to move, as components finish, new obligations arrive or, as happened in July 2026, a federal agreement is withdrawn and becomes a closeout obligation instead.

children.text: Classifying the Components

Figure 15.3 classifies each component on five attributes. Type distinguishes compliance projects, strategic projects, operational programs, analytical projects and organizational projects; the type tells you how the component should be managed. Priority is critical, high or medium. Lead names the accountable organization. The status and stage-gate column records where the component is now and the next point at which it must demonstrate progress.

The pillar column matters most for scheduling. Because the components are grouped by pillar, each inherits that pillar's inbound dependencies from the five-pillar framework. An Economics component such as reference-based-pricing implementation cannot be productively implemented before the Technology components that make it measurable, however close its own deadline is. Track 3 of this course turns that observation into scheduling rules.

The sample below shows one component from each pillar as the book recorded it for 2026. The full inventory is in Figure 15.3, and the Portfolio Sequencing Test on the platform loads all nineteen as its Vermont preset.

children.text: What the Inventory Usually Reveals

The book's Implications section describes what organizations typically discover when they build their first inventory. They are running more simultaneous transformation components than they had counted. Several components have no named owner. And two or three components sit downstream of a dependency nobody is tracking.

Vermont's inventory carries one more lesson: the portfolio function itself is a component. AHS PMO establishment appears in the Operations pillar with a critical priority and a target of being operational in the second quarter of 2027. A portfolio can, and here does, contain the component responsible for managing the portfolio, and if that component slips, everything else is managed less well.

None of these findings requires new data or new authority to produce. They come from reading documents the organization already has and writing the results in one table. That is why the book recommends the inventory as the first step for any state or organization, wherever it is in its transformation.

The inventory also changes conversations with oversight bodies. A legislature or board that receives component-by-component reports sees activity; one that receives the inventory sees the shape of the whole, including which components carry critical priority, which share a deadline, and which have no owner. That shift from activity to shape is the first sign that a portfolio is being managed rather than merely reported.

body.content: Chapter 15 presents the inventory method as directly repeatable by any organization or state agency: list every statute, grant, model agreement and initiative touching the five pillars, then map each to a pillar and an owner. The number of components will differ; the book's point is that most organizations underestimate their portfolio until they do this, because no single department sees the whole.
body.title: Beyond Vermont

children.text: An initiative without a named owner is not a component; it is a risk. Record it, and make assigning an owner the first action against it.
Build Your Own Inventory

You can build a first inventory in an afternoon. Start from the documents that impose obligations on your organization: statutes and regulations, contracts and grant agreements, board-approved plans and any regulator's directives. For a hospital, that includes payer contracts with value-based terms, state reporting obligations, and capital projects tied to the transformation.

Then enter your components into the Portfolio Sequencing Test at /portfolio-sequencing-test. The tool starts with Vermont's nineteen components; you can remove them, add your own with the + Add component button, and set each one's pillar, status and calendar target. In Track 3 you will use the same tool to run the sequencing test on your inventory. For now, the goal is a complete list with an owner and a pillar for every line.

Keep the inventory dated and revisit it at a fixed interval. A portfolio is not static: components finish, new obligations arrive, and some components should be stopped. The inventory is the document in which those changes become visible.

points: A portfolio must be defined before it can be managed: every component identified, classified and assigned governance.
Vermont has never published a portfolio definition; HTR's 19-component inventory was built from Act 68, the AHEAD agreement, the RHT application and AHS reports.
A component counts only if it has a named owner and a dated obligation, and each goes to the one pillar whose function it serves.
Each component is classified by pillar, type, priority, lead and next stage gate; the pillar determines its inbound dependencies.
Nineteen is a dated snapshot, not an official number; the inventory changes as components finish, arrive or are withdrawn.
First inventories typically reveal more components than expected, components with no owner, and untracked dependencies.
The Portfolio Sequencing Test lets you replace Vermont's components with your own and becomes the base for the sequencing work in Track 3.

Aspirations without an owner or date are not yet components; if they matter, assigning an owner is the first action, and until then they belong on the risk register.
